title: RTOS Concurrency and Real-Time Timing

standard.family: AutoLeaP Embedded Systems Body of Knowledge

A deadline is met only when execution time, blocking, release jitter, interrupt interference and higher-priority workload remain within a bounded response time. Priority assignment without a system model often produces fragile behavior that fails when diagnostics, logging or communication load changes.
learningObjectives: Explain scheduling, blocking and interference in an RTOS.
Select synchronization primitives using ownership and timing semantics.
Build a timing argument using worst-case response rather than average utilization.
explanation: An RTOS provides tasks, priorities, events, timers, synchronization and interrupt integration, but determinism is not automatic. A deadline is met only when execution time, blocking, release jitter, interrupt interference and higher-priority workload remain within a bounded response time. Priority assignment without a system model often produces fragile behavior that fails when diagnostics, logging or communication load changes.

Mutexes protect owned resources and may use priority inheritance or ceiling protocols. Semaphores signal availability, queues transfer data or ownership, and event flags represent conditions. Each primitive has overflow, timeout and failure semantics that must be designed. Long critical sections, interrupt masking and hidden driver callbacks can dominate the timing path even when the control task itself is short.

Multicore systems add shared cache, memory, interconnect and cross-core synchronization interference. Core separation is not proof of independence. The architecture should allocate budgets, define shared-resource policies and provide tracing that correlates tasks, interrupts and data age across cores.
whyItMatters: Average CPU usage can remain low while tail latency violates a hard deadline.
Explicit timing governance prevents later features from consuming invisible shared margin.
activities: Define queue capacities and overload behavior
Create timing regression and budget-change governance
automotiveExample: A 1 ms actuator task receives sensor data from an ISR and publishes status to diagnostics. Flash logging is moved to a low-priority worker with bounded buffering, while erase operations are prohibited during critical operation. The mutex protecting calibration uses a defined protocol and updates occur only in a controlled mode.
commonMistakes: Using average execution time as a deadline argument
Lowering a task priority without checking resource ownership
Performing flash or network operations inside critical sections
Assuming separate cores eliminate common-resource interference
Allowing queues to grow without overflow policy
